dataset.name: Radiocarbon of deep fine roots across four in lowland seasonal tropical forests in Panama
description: Fine roots are key to ecosystem-scale nutrient, carbon (C), and water cycling, but our understanding of fine root traits variation within and among tropical forests, one of Earth’s most C-rich ecosystems, is limited. In 2022 and 2023, we aimed to explore differences in deep root characteristics among four lowland tropical forests in Panama, which vary in fertility and mean annual precipitation. We measured radiocarbon content (fraction modern [FM] and Δ14C) and δ13C of live fine roots at depths greater than 80 cm, up to 120 cm. The goal was to understand how deep root characteristics differ across these sites.

The datasets provided include .csv and .xlsx files for radiocarbon content (fraction modern [FM] and Δ14C) and δ13C of live fine roots at depths greater than 80 cm, up to 120 cm collected from late 2017 to 2018 across four different forests. Additionally, a .kml file is provided with coordinates for all 32 plots included in the study across four forests (n = 8 plots per site). This dataset serves as baseline data before a throughfall exclusion experiment, Panama Rainforest Changes with Experimental Drying (PARCHED), was implemented. No special software is needed to open these files.

measurementTechnique:
Study Sites & Design:
This study was conducted in four distinct lowland seasonal tropical forests located across gradients in rainfall and soil fertility on the Isthmus of Panama. The sites are a subset of a larger network of ~50 1-ha long-term plots maintained by the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) in the Panamanian lowlands. The four forests span an increase of 1,000 mm MAP, and include three forests on strongly weathered, low fertility soils at low (site GIG), mid (site P12), and high rainfall (site SC), and one forest on high-fertility soils paired with the infertile forest at mid-rainfall (site P13). This design was used to help disentangle effects of mean annual precipitation (MAP) and soil fertility on soil responses to seasonal and experimental drying. The four forests included here were: a forest at 2350 mm MAP on strongly weathered, infertile soil on the Gigante Peninsula (GIG), two paired forests at 2500 mm MAP on the Buena Vista Peninsula, one with strongly weathered infertile soil (Plot 12 [P12]), and one with less weathered fertile soil (Plot 13 [P13]), and a forest at 3300 mm MAP on strongly weathered infertile soil on the Caribbean coast in the San Lorenzo forest at Sherman Crane (SC). More information about the sites can be found in other publications (Dietterich and others, 2022; Cusack and others, 2023a; Cusack and others, 2023b)

Data Collection for this data set:
Root samples were collected during late 2017 to 2018 across four different sites (GIG, P12, P13 and SC) at depths greater than 80 cm, up to 120 cm. Roots were separated in live fine roots less than 2 mm in diameter at 4-5 plots per site. Roots were cleaned, then dried at 60°C until a constant weight was achieved and ground. Live fine roots were prepared for radiocarbon analysis using sealed-tube combustion to CO2 in the presence of copper oxide (CuO) and silver (Ag), followed by cryogenic purification and reduction to graphite on Fe powder in the presence of H2 (Vogel et al., 1984). The δ13C values were measured on a split of purified CO2 at the Stable Isotope Geosciences Facility at Texas A&M University using a Thermo Scientific MAT 253 Dual Inlet Stable Isotope Ratio Mass Spectrometer. The 14C samples were measured as graphite using the 10 MV Van de Graaff FN or the 1MV NEC Compact accelerator mass spectrometer at Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory (Broek et al., 2021). The 14C values were corrected for mass-dependent fractionation using measured δ13C values and are reported as Δ14C corrected to the year of analysis (2022 or 2023) and as fraction modern (FM or F14C) (Reimer et al., 2004).
